content:
Nat.Primes is currently defined as a subtype { n // Nat.Prime n}, and this subtype defeq is relied upon frequently in the 17 files in Mathlib using Nat.Primes, for instance to construct Nat.Primes.prodNatEquiv, or to gain access to various lemmas such as Summable.subtype or Subtype.coe_injective. It all works, but (as recently suggested by @Jireh Loreaux at https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/41419#discussion_r3540242569) conceptually one could instead rely on a Function.Embedding from Nat.Primes to Nat with an associated coercion, a constructor (Nat.Prime.toPrimes?), and replacing all uses of Subtype API with their Function.Embedding analogues (creating such analogues as needed). It's a moderately large chore, but I think with an AI agent this is doable.

My question is whether this is a worthwhile exercise for Mathlib. It wouldn't make any noticeable improvements in performance or expressivity; the gains are more philosophical in nature (and perhaps making the Nat.Primes API more robust to future changes).
could we make Nat.Primes an abbrev?

We could, though my understanding is that abbrevs are discouraged in Mathlib.

One thing about Nat.Primes is that it is a very "bare" type with few instances that it doesn't automatically inherit from Nat; for instance, it isn't a Monoid or AddMonoid. But it shows up somewhat frequently in analytic number theory as the domain of various functions, e.g., it is common to consider sums or products over primes. Though Mathlib is not fully consistent about embracing it: for instance, Nat.factorization is defined as a Finsupp on Nat rather than Nat.Primes (and Nat.factorizationEquiv becomes slightly awkward as a consequence). So this type is in some sort of purgatory between a first-class Mathlib object and an optional abbrev for a Subtype. It's not clear to me whether its status should be upgraded (as the preferred domain for functions over primes), downgraded (to a mere abbrev), or left as is.

I think it's not unreasonable for Nat.Primes to be an abbrev. To say that they are discouraged in Mathlib is not really correct; we just want abbrevs precisely when they are useful. The most essential question is: are there any instances we don't want to inherit? If there are none, an abbrev is reasonable, and then the question is: do we want to construct an API barrier here? That's always a bit more finicky to decide.

PNat is somewhat similar to Nat.Primes, with a comparably modest API, and is currently a def rather than an abbrev. I guess they should be treated more or less similarly. (Actually, from a mathematical perspective, it is slightly more logical to define Nat.Primes as a subtype of PNat rather than Nat, though I can imagine that this makes life more difficult for Lean, especially given that the tactic suite (e.g., omega) is much more optimized for Nat than for PNat.)

One other option is to def or abbrev Nat.Primes to be the Set Nat object { n | Nat.Prime n} rather than the Subtype Nat object { n // Nat.Prime n }. With the implicit coercion from sets to subtypes, this would not significantly affect most of the current usage of Nat.Primes but would also allow one to use this notation to access the set of primes (otherwise one has to use some awkward construction such as Subtype.val '' (Set.univ : Set Nat.Primes)). (Also, much of the Subtype API currently only works if the subtype was coerced from a Set to begin with.)

I haven't used the set/type of primes enough to know whether it's more often used as subset of (p)nats, or as a standalone type. Does one of these uses dominate?

Or should they both exist, and both have some dedicated API?

I think Nat.Primes is almost unused. It may be useful to keep things elementary (i.e. not importing a lot of ring theory, but note that even the definition of Prime requires some imports), but not much more than that.
I mean that Nat.Prime is defined via Irreducible, so I don't think we are very much interested to keep things elementary.

Nat.Prime is used in ~78 files in Mathlib, while Nat.Primes is used in ~15 files (this is a crude search, numbers not guaranteed to be accurate). The latter most naturally appears in files such as SumPrimeReciprocals.lean where one is considering sums or products over primes (though arguably one could replace Nat.Primes: Subtype Nat throughout with { n | Nat.Prime n}with no great loss). But these numbers reflect current usage rather than "natural" usage; I suspect many places in which Nat.Prime currently appears could be refactored to also utilize Nat.Primes in an organic way.

The one place where I think Nat.Primes would make particular sense is in Nat.factorizationEquiv, which is currently of type ℕ+ ≃ { f : ℕ →₀ ℕ // ∀ p ∈ f.support, Prime p } but could be of type ℕ+ ≃ Nat.Primes →₀ ℕ, or even ℕ+ ≃* Multiplicative (Nat.Primes →₀ ℕ) instead (this would be a substantial refactor though). This to me is a more conceptually clear reification of the fundamental theorem of arithmetic. Though even here one could use ↑{ n | Nat.Prime n} in place of Nat.Primes. Still, the current version is awkward, which is perhaps why Nat.factorizationEquiv is almost totally unused. (There are also other variants such as {q : ℚ // 0 < q} ≃ Nat.Primes →₀ ℤ that might be useful.)
Are there any instances that Nat.Primes type would have installed that differ from what it inherits via Subtype.foo instances?

Terence Tao said:

Nat.Prime is used in ~78 files in Mathlib, while Nat.Primes is used in ~15 files (this is a crude search, numbers not guaranteed to be accurate).

Side remark: you can get an accurate count by right-clicking on either name in Mathlib and clicking "Find all references". This gives the following.
Nat.Prime is used 1170 times in 214 files
Nat.Primes is used 95 times in 16 files

Yakov Pechersky said:

Are there any instances that Nat.Primes type would have installed that differ from what it inherits via Subtype.foo instances?

The only one I can think of is docs#Nat.Primes.infinite (Euclid's theorem), though this is admittedly a pretty fundamental one.
Infinite can't be inherited via Subtype so it is fine
I can't even think of a data-carrying instance (aside from decidability) that we can add to Nat.Primes
Oh it can have linear order but that obviously should be inherited from Nat
One could also make Nat.Primes an abbrev for PrimeSpectrum ℤ, but somehow I think this will make absolutely everyone unhappy :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:

Unfortunately 0 is a prime ideal whose generator is not prime...

More seriously, Nat.Primes.infinite could be very well stated defining the type on the fly, or even using Set.Infinite, that seems more natural to me.
I think we have the Set.Infinite version separately
I think Nat.Primes.infinite is justified by the existence of Nat.Primes, not vice versa

Terence Tao said:

Nat.Prime is used in ~78 files in Mathlib

Nat.Prime is used everywhere, its most common form is [Fact p.Prime]
I think some advantage of Nat.Primes being a Type is one can setup some instances on it, for example (p : Nat.Primes) -> Fact p.1.Prime and NeZero p.1 etc.
All of these would of course still be true if we made it an abbrev
